report:
Your assessment is correct: **the claim that soursop cures cancer in humans is false.**

### Evidence Supporting the Claim (Laboratory Studies)
Laboratory (*in vitro*) and animal (*in vivo*) research demonstrates that soursop (*Annona muricata*, or graviola) contains bioactive compounds—notably annonaceous acetogenins—that show cytotoxic, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory activity against certain cancer cell lines, including breast and liver cells ([News-Medical](https://www.news-medical.net/health/Soursop-Nutrition-Bioactive-Compounds-and-Human-Health.aspx)).

### Evidence Against the Claim (Human Trials & Medical Consensus)
* **Lack of Clinical Evidence:** Major oncology institutions, including Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, emphasize that there is a complete absence of completed human clinical trials demonstrating that soursop can treat or cure cancer in humans ([MSKCC](https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/graviola); [Outcomes4Me](https://outcomes4me.com/cancer-topic/nutrition/soursop-and-cancer-separating-miracle-claims-from-science/)). Laboratory findings in test tubes frequently fail to translate into effective or safe human treatments.
* **Safety Risks:** Medical experts warn against using soursop extracts as a treatment. Soursop contains neurotoxins such as annonacin, which can cause nerve damage and movement disorders resembling Parkinson's disease with high or prolonged intake ([CancerCenter.com](https://www.cancercenter.com/community/blog/2017/07/experts-warn-against-soursop-fruit-to-fight-cancer)).

### Conclusion
While soursop extracts display preliminary anticancer mechanisms in laboratory dishes and animal models, there is no clinical evidence that soursop cures cancer in humans. Medical authorities advise against using it as an alternative cancer therapy due to unproven efficacy and potential neurotoxicity.
